newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMU not bad for jobs, says EU commissioner.
newsitem.headline: EMU not bad for jobs, says EU commissioner.

text.p: European Employment Commissioner Padraig Flynn dismissed on Thursday the idea that monetary union was bad for jobs, saying Denmark showed it was possible to cut the budget deficit and lower unemployment at the same time.
Denmark has succeeded in keeping its currency stable and in reducing the budget deficit while maintaining the level of social welfare benefits, he said.
"At the same time as all of that happened they have reduced unemployment quite dramatically," Flynn told Reuters. "It... shows that EMU in no way destabilises or creates unemployment."
"Denmark has made exceptional progress during the last few years in the fight against unemployment," he said.
Flynn was hosting a seminar on recent reforms in the Danish labour market, which the European Commission said had resulted in a decline in the country's jobless rate.

Critics of the EU's plans to introduce monetary union say the project may further undermine employment as governments desperately seek to bring down their budget deficits to qualify from the start in 1999.
The Danish government has stressed the need to meet the Maastricht criteria even though the country rejected EMU membership in a 1993 referendum.
It is one of only three EU countries which currently seem to qualify for EMU. Ireland and Luxembourg also meet the criteria.

Flynn praised Copenhagen's labour market policies, which are focused on training to boost skills and bring long-term unemployed back into the workforce, as a "great example" which other EU countries could learn from.

"The Danish experience has shown that is is possible to help the unemployed back into the mainstream of society, without jeopardising the stability of its currency, minimum standards of social protection, or aggravating the gaps between the rich and poor," a Commission statement said.

The seminar was taking place at the same day as the Danish National Statistics Office said that the country's seasonally adjusted unemployment rose to 9.1 percent in July from 8.7 percent the previous month.
However, it was still down from last year's level of 10.6 percent and below the EU average of 10.8 percent.
According to Commission figures, the Danish jobless rate has declined to 6.4 percent from 8.7 percent over three years.

Danish Labour Minister Jytte Andersen told the seminar about the reforms introduced by the Social Demoratic-led government in 1994, representing a more active and effective labour market policy following the steady rise in unemployment in the 1980s.
